faq.q: Why does my body give off infrared?
faq.a: Everything warm sends out infrared light, which our eyes cannot see. At about 37 degrees Celsius, your body glows brightly in infrared compared with cooler walls and plants.
asks: What does a motion sensor detect?

faq.q: What is the bumpy plastic dome on a motion sensor?
faq.a: It is a Fresnel lens, made of many small lens sections. It splits the view into separate zones and focuses each onto the sensor, so walking between zones makes the signal jump.

faq.q: How does a PIR sensor tell that something is moving?
faq.a: PIR means passive infrared. The sensor has two halves wired so they cancel out; a still room affects both equally, but someone moving makes one half warmer than the other for a moment.

faq.q: Why do motion sensor lights switch off when I stand still?
faq.a: The sensor only notices changes in infrared. If you stand still, nothing changes, so when the timer runs out the light goes off. A wave of your arm brings it back.
asks: Why does the light go off if I don't move?

faq.q: Can a motion sensor be fooled?
faq.a: Yes. Pets, passing cars with warm engines or warm air from a vent can set one off, because they also change the infrared reaching the sensor. Sensitivity and aiming settings help.
asks: Why does my outside light switch on by itself?

facts: PIR stands for passive infrared: the sensor sends nothing out, it only receives.
The human body gives off most of its infrared at wavelengths of around 10 micrometres, far longer than visible light.
